const r = await tools.exec_command({cmd:"cat > /tmp/peerage-design-luna.md <<'EOF'
# Peerage alias design

## Recommendation

Add a derived, in-memory `PeerageAliasIndex` owned by `ResolutionInput`. Build it once from the complete validated observation set in `ResolutionInput::new`, after duplicate IDs and payment-role references have been checked. Do not persist it in cleaned Parquet, resolved output, or a new table. This is run-local contextual evidence, not a canonical identity declaration. The existing source rows and digest remain the audit record.

The index records only aliases backed by an explicit peerage bridge. Its canonical key is the normalized peerage designation, retaining every designation token such as `of Turville`; its value is the normalized full personal form derived from the bridge. It also indexes the bridge's explicit personal spelling to that same derived full form. A designation with bridges to more than one distinct personal name is ambiguous and contributes no mappings. Repeated equivalent bridges collapse after existing name normalization, including the source's extra inner whitespace.

For the supplied evidence, the one unambiguous bridge is `Baron Sainsbury of Turville (David Sainsbury)`. It establishes `David Sainsbury of Turville`. The parser maps `Lord Sainsbury of Turville`, `Lord David Sainsbury of Turville`, the Baron bridge spelling, and plain `David Sainsbury` to that form. This is an exact designation and explicit-name relation, not a surname or `of` heuristic. Francesca/Perrin remain separate because neither appears in that bridge relation.

## Domain shape and ownership

`funder_name.rs` owns peerage parsing because it already owns `PersonTitle`, normalization, balanced-parenthesis extraction, and evidence-derived name features. Add a peerage-specific parsed form rather than loosening `ParsedPersonName` or stripping titles from arbitrary names. The parsed designation retains the complete normalized tail. The lead token vocabulary is exhaustive and peerage-specific (`Lord`, `Baron`); it must not turn ordinary `lord`/`baron` text elsewhere into a person alias. Validate bridge contents as a simple personal name with the existing personal-name character constraints, and reject unbalanced or multiple-content annotations. Keep the original source spelling intact.

`ResolutionInput` owns the contextual index because it sees the whole run and is already the boundary that validates observations and role references. Suggested private shape:

```rust
struct PeerageAliasIndex {
    by_observation: BTreeMap<FunderObservationId, BTreeSet<PeeragePersonName>>,
}
```

Build a temporary `designation -> BTreeSet<bridge person>` map from eligible bridge observations. Keep only singleton sets. Resolve each eligible observation's parsed peerage designation or exact bridge-person spelling through that map and store the derived alias under its ID. No schema changes are needed. Avoid adding a string field to each observation: doing so would serialize derived contextual state into a source artifact and obscure its provenance.

Use a typed normalized `PeeragePersonName` (or equivalent private newtype) so parser output, index keys, blocking values, and equality checks share one normalization contract. Keep title parsing finite and exhaustive. Do not add duplicate title allowlists in callers; the peerage parser should match the canonical title enum exhaustively, with `Baron` added to that enum if it is a recognized peerage title.

## Shared evidence path

Expose one `ResolutionInput` method that returns the eligible peerage aliases for an observation. `scoring_input`'s `blocking_keys` uses that method to emit a namespaced exact key, for example `individual-peerage-name:<normalized full form>`. The identity classifier uses the same method and links only when the two observations share an indexed alias. This makes candidate generation and final acceptance use the same evidence source.

Apply role/kind gates in that shared method: both the bridge source and each aliased observation must be `FunderRole::Donor` and `EntityKind::Person` (`Individual`/`Person`). Never use peerage evidence for payer or ultimate-payer rows, and never use it to connect organizations or unknown kinds. Keep the current person-versus-organization conflict checks and component anchor checks; peerage evidence is a supporting name link, not a replacement for those safeguards. Add a dedicated `LinkEvidence::PeerageAlias` only if output provenance needs to distinguish the basis; otherwise the existing extracted-name basis is enough, but tests must pin the chosen externally visible reason/basis.

Do not add aliases to `Observation.alias_normalized`, which are explicit source trading-as aliases and are serialized as cleaned evidence. Mixing these separate evidence classes there would erase the evidence distinction.

## Candidate comparison

A reviewed peerage registry would make approved mappings explicit and easy to inspect, but it duplicates data policy outside the source corpus, needs ongoing curation, and would encode these people/designations as hand-maintained special cases. It does not meet the requested generic, evidence-derived behavior. The derived context index is smaller: one parser, one run-local index, one shared lookup, and no migration. It abstains automatically when source bridges conflict.

A broad title-stripping or surname-based variant rule is smaller in lines but unsafe. It can merge distinct people and loses the peerage designation that disambiguates this case. Reject both approaches.

## Behavioral proof to require during implementation

Extend the existing real capture-to-clean-to-resolve CLI integration test in `exposed/tests/declaration_resolution_cli.rs`, using distinct declarations and individual donor captures. Include both Lord spellings, the Baron explicit bridge (including the whitespace variant), and plain David spelling. Assert all five share one run-local identity, the accepted pair evidence is recorded, their donor attributions remain attached to their original funding entries, and the raw/cleaned artifacts remain byte-identical after resolve. Include the known Francesca/Perrin observations and assert they remain distinct. Include two incompatible explicit bridge names for one designation and assert the context index abstains, so the related peerage forms do not gain an automatic link. Include payer/ultimate-payer and non-person controls to prove the gates.

The regression must pass through the native CLI resolver with its real candidate blocker and scorer; a unit test of the parser alone cannot prove a candidate was generated. For the HTTP-facing proof, load the same resolved artifact through the actual ingestion/load path, start the app with the test harness, and assert through the public funder/member HTTP response that the merged identity is exposed once with the expected source names and occurrence count. Use the existing `latest_ingestion.rs` or `exposed/tests/integration.rs` application harness rather than a mocked handler. If the HTTP projection intentionally omits aliases or member links, assert the externally available identity field and document that field in the test. Do not change resolution schema or API solely to expose internal peerage evidence.

## Scope and proof limits

The source bridge is the only authority for the derived relation. A bridge whose designation or personal name cannot be parsed conservatively is ignored. A conflicting bridge set yields no derived alias for that designation. Exact canonical designation matching retains `of Turville` and does not generalize to another peerage or surname. This intentionally favors missed links over unsupported merges.
EOF",workdir:"/Users/jamie/development/exposed.resolve-peerage-name-variants",max_output_tokens:1000}); text(r.output);

content.text:
Design saved at `/tmp/peerage-design-luna.md`. It recommends a run-local `PeerageAliasIndex` on `ResolutionInput`, built only from unambiguous explicit parenthetical bridges. One shared lookup supplies both candidate blocking and identity decisions, with donor and person gates. It avoids schema changes and rejects broad title stripping, surname matching, and a hand-maintained registry.

The design also specifies CLI and HTTP integration proof, including conflicting bridges, Francesca/Perrin separation, and payer and non-person controls. No repository files were changed.
